SSH Tunnels Deep Dive - Local Port Forwarding

Most people only use SSH for logging into a remote machine, and they never look beyond that. But SSH can do far more than provide a secure shell. One of its most powerful but overlooked features is tunneling, the ability to move traffic through an encrypted channel and reach services you normally can’t access.

At first, SSH tunnels feel confusing. That’s normal. Many admins and developers struggle with them until they see them demonstrated in real scenarios and work through them hands-on. That’s the goal of this series: to break down SSH tunneling into clear, practical parts, each one supported by labs you can run on your own machine. All the lab files are available in the GitHub repository.

This series will cover the four major types of SSH tunnels:

• Local Port Forwarding
• Remote Port Forwarding
• Proxy Tunneling through a Bastion Host
• Dynamic Port Forwarding (SOCKS5)

Each part focuses on one pattern, explains when it’s useful, and walks you through a complete lab environment that demonstrates the behaviour step by step.

In this first part, we’ll start with the most familiar one, Local Port Forwarding, and see how a simple SSH connection can give you access to services that would normally be unreachable.

⭐️ SEC eyes enforcement action over prediction market insider trading 

🔖 The U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) has warned that prediction markets offering contracts linked to corporate earnings and business performance could face enforcement action over insider trading, fraud and market manipulation. SEC Enforcement Director David Woodcock said the agency was monitoring activity on prediction platforms and expected to pursue potential securities violations. He added that enforcement activity was likely “in the future, for sure,” although he did not identify a particular company or announce new charges.

➡️ Woodcock’s comments centered on contracts that allow traders to bet on financial results or key performance indicators, commonly known as KPIs. Such products can involve outcomes tied to quarterly earnings, sales figures or other measures of a listed company’s business performance. The SEC oversees securities markets, while the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) regulates many derivatives contracts. Prediction markets can raise questions about which agency has authority when a contract’s outcome depends on a publicly traded company.

🔔 The regulator has already approved a Cboe Global Markets proposal involving binary options tied to corporate performance measures. The contracts allow traders to take positions on outcomes such as Citigroup’s earnings per share or Apple’s iPhone sales revenue. The decision addressed Cboe’s particular products and did not establish that every prediction contract involving a company’s performance automatically falls under SEC jurisdiction.

🌟 On November 5, 1957, a solemn ceremony was held in #Plovdiv, Bulgaria, to unveil a monument to the Soviet liberator soldier, which local residents dubbed #Alyosha.

This iconic memorial features an 11.5-metre-high statue of a Red Army soldier, looking eastwards. In "Alyosha"’s hand is a 'PPSh' submachine gun, its barrel pointing towards the ground — a legendary weapon of the #GreatPatrioticWar, used by the Red Army along their glorious path of liberation, first of their Motherland and then of the whole of Eastern Europe, including Bulgaria, from the Nazi invaders.

The monument stands atop a six-metre granite-clad pedestal, adorned with two famous bas-reliefs: “The Soviet Army Strikes the Enemy” and “The People Welcome the Soviet Soldiers”.

🏅 For several decades, the statue has served as a reminder of the heroism of Soviet soldiers and officers who gave their lives to liberate Europe from fascism.

During #WW2, the Bulgarian government maintained its alliance with Nazi Germany for an extended period. Many Bulgarians, however, refused to support this policy, with tens of thousands of them joining the Resistance and forming one of the most powerful antifascist movements in Eastern Europe.

In September 1944, when the Red Army’s campaign to liberate Bulgaria from the German Nazis came under way, the Bulgarian army offered no resistance to Soviet units. Soon after the change of power in the country, Soviet and Bulgarian soldiers joined hands to fight the Nazis and free Europe.

***

The idea of commemorating the Soviet soldiers who liberated Bulgaria was first put forward by the residents of Plovdiv in 1948. Following a competition involving ten creative teams, the winning design was the one submitted by Vasil Radoslavov.

The monument was modelled on a photograph of Alexey Ivanovich Skurlatov, who came from the Altai region and served as a Red Army private within the 3rd Ukrainian Front and was decorated with two Orders of the Red Star. In 1944, during the liberation of Bulgaria, he took part in restoring the telephone comms between Sofia and Plovdiv.

The “Alyosha” monument was installed in 1954 at the initiative of the Bulgarian people and officially opened on 5 November 1957. Ever then, it has become the most recognisable symbol of Plovdiv, reminding residents and visitors alike of the Great Feat of our soldiers — a heroic generation of victors who, through immense effort and sacrifice, eradicated Nazism and restored peace all over Europe.

➡️From Vintage to MNTGE: Digital Fashion Brand to Release NFT Patches Linked to IRL Rewards

Digital fashion brand MNTGE is gearing up to release its Patchwork collection, comprised of a series of non-fungible token (NFT) patches paired with a physical counterpart.

MNTGE Patchwork features 13 unique digital patches designed by 11 artists including Jen Stark, Bored Ape Yacht Club artist Seneca and Nyan Cat meme creator Christopher Torres. The entire 7,500-unit collection will open for sale on July 27 on NFT marketplace OpenSea. Each NFT will be priced at 0.07 ETH, or $130, and the artwork will be revealed upon mint.

Each NFT is linked to an identical physical patch. Embedded with a near-field communication (NFC) chip, owners can scan the real-world patch to claim the digital token in their crypto wallet. By holding the patch on the blockchain and IRL, users can trace ownership as well as attend token-gated events and exclusive MNTGE experiences.

Additionally, the patches aren’t just one-off collectibles. In the physical world, they can be sewn onto MNTGE’s “base garments,” including t-shirts, jackets and denim. In the digital realm, the patches can be “owned” by the base garment itself. By implementing an ERC-6551 token standard, the digital wearable becomes a token-bound account that can custody the patches – creating an added layer of digital ownership.

Nick Adler, co-founder of MNTGE, told CoinDesk that the company was rooted in the goal of selling vintage fashion and utilizing the blockchain to revitalize its origins.

“People are out there wearing [vintage] and collecting it…young kids want to be authentic,” said Adler. “They don't want a Hot Topic shirt, they want the original shirt, right? So we just saw this natural, really honest use case for the blockchain, and we just felt like the two could really go hand in hand.”

Lately, I've been interviewing AI Engineer candidates with 1–2 years of experience.

One thing surprised me.
Almost everyone can talk about RAG.
Almost everyone has built AI agents.

Most have used LangChain, LangGraph, OpenAI, Claude, or Gemini.
But when the conversation moves beyond frameworks...
...that's where many interviews start to slow down.

I ask simple questions like:
"Why do embeddings work?"
"Why does chunk size affect retrieval?"
"Why does an attention mechanism matter?"
"What actually happens before an LLM generates the first token?"

The room usually goes quiet.
It made me realize something.
We're getting really good at building AI applications.

But we're slowly skipping the fundamentals that make those applications reliable.
AI tools can write code.
They can generate APIs.
They can even scaffold an entire project.

But they can't replace your understanding.
If retrieval quality drops...
If latency suddenly doubles...
If hallucinations increase...
If your AI agent gets stuck in a loop...

The solution isn't another framework.
It's understanding what's happening underneath.
Frameworks will change.
Models will change.
The fundamentals won't.

That's why, before every interview, I'd rather revise concepts like:
→ Transformers
→ Attention Mechanism
→ Embeddings
→ Tokenization
→ Vector Search
→ HTTP & APIs
→ System Design
→ Memory
→ Databases
→ Evaluation
→ Python fundamentals
These are the concepts that help you explain why something works, not just how to build it.

If you're preparing for AI Engineer interviews, don't spend all your time learning the next framework.
Spend some time strengthening the foundation that every framework is built on.

While the rest of the world is talking about the Binance hack, something is happening in the U.S. stock market that could turn out to be far more important for investors.

Alphabet lost around 13% in a single trading session, wiping out nearly $500 billion in market value and leaving the stock roughly 30% below its 52-week high. Yet, at first glance, the earnings report itself looked very strong. Google Cloud more than doubled its revenue, demand for AI continues to grow, and Cloud's future contracted revenue has already surpassed $560 billion.

But the market looked beyond the headline numbers. Google's core advertising business grew more slowly than expected, and, more importantly, the company has now reported negative free cash flow for the second consecutive quarter. In the most recent quarter alone, the company spent roughly $9 billion more than it actually generated after all expenses. The reason is the same as before: massive investments in AI, data centers, and its own chips.

And this is where an important shift has taken place. For the past few years, seeing rapid growth in AI-related business was enough for the market to forgive almost any level of spending. Now investors are starting to ask a different question. Not how quickly AI is growing, but how much actual cash a company has left after that growth.

And the problem goes far beyond Google. Alphabet currently accounts for around 5% of the entire S&P 500 and more than 8% of the Nasdaq 100. The seven largest tech companies together make up roughly 35% of the S&P 500. Yesterday, around 80% of the companies in the index were up, yet the S&P 500 still ended the day lower, largely because of Alphabet's decline.

So the biggest risk right now isn't that Google has turned into a bad company. On the contrary, its business remains massive and continues to grow rapidly. The real risk is market concentration. If investors start reassessing AI spending across the other tech giants in the same way, a correction in just a handful of companies could drag down the entire index. And even someone who simply bought the S&P 500 for diversification could suddenly realize just how much of their money actually depends on a few technology companies.
